title: Working Scientifically

standard_text: Pose questions and make predictions; plan and conduct fair tests safely; use equipment to measure and record observations in tables and graphs; identify patterns; and communicate findings (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Year 4 science inquiry content descriptions).
meta_desc: Free Year 4 science worksheets on working scientifically: testable questions, predictions, fair tests, reading rulers and thermometers, tables, column graphs and conclusions. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Change one thing and measure carefully.
key_sub: A fair test changes only one thing; careful measuring makes results reliable.
body_html:
How to think about it

Scientists ask a question, make a prediction and test it fairly.

  • Change only one thing and keep everything else the same.
  • Measure with the right tool (ruler, thermometer, stopwatch, scales) and write the unit.
  • Record results in a table, look for a pattern, and write a conclusion that matches the results.
Example

Which tool measures temperature?

temperature is measured in °C

Answer: a thermometer

Example

Ball bounces: 54, 56, 55 cm. Reliable?

the results are close together

Answer: yes

Common mistakes

  • Changing more than one thing in a test.
  • Reading the wrong mark on a scale.
  • Forgetting to write units such as cm or °C.

faq.a: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same, so you know what caused the result.
Repeating tests checks that the results are reliable. If one result is very different, test again.

faq.q: What is the difference between a prediction and a conclusion?
faq.a: A prediction is what you think will happen before the test. A conclusion says what the results showed.

items.q: Is this an observation or an inference (an explanation)? “The nail in salt water had the most rust after a week.”

items.e: An observation is what you saw or measured; an inference explains it.

items.q: What is a variable in an investigation?
